lesson.title: Anorexia Nervosa: When Restriction Becomes Danger
lesson.summary: Anorexia nervosa involves restricting food intake to a significantly low body weight, combined with an intense fear of gaining weight and a genuine disturbance in how body weight and shape are experienced.
lesson.body:
Anorexia nervosa is defined by three interlocking features. First, restriction of energy intake relative to what the body needs, leading to a significantly low body weight given the person's age, sex, developmental stage, and physical health. Second, an intense fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, or persistent behavior that interferes with weight gain, even though the person is already at a significantly low weight. Third, a disturbance in the way body weight or shape is experienced, an undue influence of body weight or shape on self-evaluation, or a persistent failure to recognize the seriousness of the current low body weight. Clinicians recognize two patterns: a restricting type, where weight loss is achieved mainly through dieting, fasting, or excessive exercise, and a binge-eating/purging type, where the person also engages in recurrent binge eating or purging behavior.

It helps to ask why restriction takes hold and becomes so difficult to reverse. For many people, restricting food initially provides a powerful sense of control or mastery, especially at a time when other parts of life feel unpredictable or overwhelming. But starvation itself is not psychologically neutral. It changes brain function and cognition in ways that tend to deepen the disorder rather than resolve the distress that started it. This is not just theory. A well known study from the 1940s, sometimes called the Minnesota Starvation Experiment, placed healthy young men with no history of eating disorders on a semi-starvation diet and found that food restriction alone, regardless of a person's prior psychology, produced intense preoccupation with food, rigid and obsessive thinking, and irritability. That finding helps explain why anorexia nervosa can become a self-reinforcing cycle: the very act of restricting reshapes thinking in ways that make continued restriction feel more urgent, not less.

The connection to hunger and eating behavior is worth making explicit. Under normal circumstances, hunger and satiety are governed by a tightly coordinated biological system, involving hypothalamic signaling and hormones such as ghrelin and leptin, that reliably motivates eating when the body needs energy. Anorexia nervosa is striking, and clinically difficult to treat, precisely because it involves a sustained psychological override of that powerful biological drive. This is also why the body image disturbance at the heart of the disorder is not vanity. Someone with anorexia nervosa can be at a critically low, medically dangerous weight and still perceive their body as normal or even overweight. That is a genuine perceptual and cognitive disturbance, not a matter of the person simply refusing to see reality.

The medical consequences of prolonged starvation are serious and touch nearly every organ system. They can include cardiac complications such as an abnormally slow heart rate or dangerous arrhythmias linked to electrolyte imbalance, and loss of bone density, which is especially concerning in adolescence, a period when peak bone mass is still being built. Anorexia nervosa is widely recognized in the clinical literature as having one of the highest mortality rates of any psychiatric disorder, which is part of why treatment often needs to begin with medical stabilization.

Anorexia nervosa most often emerges during adolescence, sometimes following a period of ordinary dieting that gradually becomes something else entirely. Because of the medical risks involved, treatment typically combines close medical monitoring with specialized psychotherapy, such as family-based treatment for adolescents, and sometimes requires a higher level of care, including inpatient or residential treatment, when a person's physical health has become unstable.
